title: Connect with Library Digital Collections at the 2026 National Book Festival
content:
Today’s guest post is from Abby Shelton, a Digital Collections Specialist & By the People community manager at the Library of Congress.

It’s the best time of year! The National Book Festival is coming up on Saturday, August 22 at the Walter E. Washington Convention Center in Washington, DC. Come see your friendly digital collections staff at our table in the Exhibit Hall.

We’ll be at the Festival from 9:00am-6:00pm talking about web archiving, how you can transcribe historical documents with By the People, and what kinds of Library of Congress collections you can find online. Read on to learn more about the activities we have planned, the knowledgeable staff who would love to talk with you, and the giveaways you can pick up. The Festival is free and open to the public, however you must reserve a free ticket in advance to attend in person. Register for your ticket today!

title: When Open Data Comes Full Circle: New OCR Reprocessing Software and Datasets Portal for Chronicling America
content:
Today’s guest post is from Nathan Yarasavage of the Serial and Government Publications Division at the Library of Congress.

True open-source collaboration is built on a simple principle: paying it forward. Last year, the Library of Congress announced a project to improve the quality of the Optical Character Recognition (OCR) text from some of the first newspapers digitized for Chronicling America. Now we are sharing our code. The NDNP-Open-OCR software is officially live on GitHub. This open-source release gives everyone access to a highly accurate, cost-effective, scalable OCR reprocessing solution that uses advanced layout detection to improve text quality.

To show what this new pipeline can do, we’ve already reprocessed over 425,000 pages and launched the brand-new Chronicling America Datasets portal. This new page provides direct access to our newly upgraded OCR text. It also serves as a gateway to downloadable bulk files for all 23+ million pages of historic news in the collection, opening new possibilities for computational research.

title: A Connection Between the Past and the Future: The Local History & Genealogy Web Archive
content:
The Local History and Genealogy Web Archive preserves websites that help researchers trace family histories and better understand the communities where their ancestors lived. In this interview, Ahmed Johnson discusses the importance of preserving the websites of local history and genealogical societies, the challenges of building a broadly representative collection, and the role of web archiving in connecting future researchers with the past.  

This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 

Please introduce yourself. What is your job at the Library of Congress, and what was your role in creating the collection? 

I am a reference librarian in the Local History and Genealogy Section at the Library of Congress, specializing in African American genealogy. I have worked at the Library for more than thirty years, beginning as a work-study student while I was still in high school. Even after leaving for college, I continued returning during school breaks because I never wanted to give up the opportunity to work here. My first position was as a deck attendant, retrieving materials requested by researchers.

title: Advocating for Digital Accessibility: An Interview with Junior Fellow Mia Giancola
content:
In this interview, 2026 Library of Congress Junior Fellow Mia Giancola discusses working on the Year of Digital Accessibility in the Library’s IT Design & Development Directorate. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Pedro: It’s great to have you on our team this summer. Could you tell us what you are working on?

Mia: Hi! I’m so excited to be here! I’d love to: I am a Junior Fellow working on the Digital Accessibility Team in the Design Division. The Digital Accessibility Team runs an accessibility educational initiative every year called the “Year of.” This year is the “Year of Magnification.” A great way to think of magnification is pinch and zoom, which many people use daily. Magnification is important when considering low vision or blind users, older adults, smartphone users, and several other key populations. In addition to informational materials, I have created an interactive game to help demonstrate the ways magnification can impact how people access digital content, including library resources and collections.

title: Transcription Can Bring People Together: A Reflection from Shelby Kruger
content:
Today’s guest post is from Shelby Kruger, a 2026 Junior Fellow at the Library of Congress. Shelby is an M.S.L.S. student at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.

If I handed you one of Walt Whitman’s early drafts, would you be able to read it? What about a handwritten letter to Abraham Lincoln? Or a diary from the American Revolution? In each of these documents, you might find challenging details to decipher: strange script, S’s that look like F’s, or unknown abbreviations. I encountered each of these elements of historic handwriting during my internship with the Digital Collections Management and Services Division this summer.

title: New Online at the Library of Congress: July 2026
content:
The Library of Congress holds the world’s preeminent body of primary-source materials for the study of the life and work of George and Ira Gershwin, providing a nearly comprehensive record of their music and lyrics, as well as correspondence, photographs, business and financial papers, publicity materials, and press accounts.

This new digital collection primarily features their music (piano-vocal scores, orchestrations, and sketches) and handwritten lyric sheets and librettos. There are also manuscripts, lyric sheets, published sheet music, both concert and theater programs, and at least one self-portrait oil painting of Ira Gershwin smoking a cigarette. What other treasures can you find?

Community Collections Grants from the American Folklife Center supported contemporary cultural field research from 2022-2024. Read more about the program on loc.gov.

title: Saving Tangible Media for Tomorrow: A Reflection from Natalie Nemes
content:
Today’s guest post is from Natalie Nemes, a 2026 Junior Fellow at the Library of Congress. Natalie recently received her Master’s in Library & Information Science from the University of Wisconsin-Madison.

When I tell people that I intern at the Library of Congress reformatting obsolete media such as CDs, DVDs, and floppy disks, their first question usually is “CDs are considered obsolete?”

CDs aren’t obsolete in the same way that 8-inch floppy disks are because we still have plenty of playback equipment for them lying around. If you want to look at the files on that old CD that’s been sitting in a shoebox for the last ten years, you probably still can — either by using a disk reader you already have, borrowing one from a friend, or buying one for a small amount of money. But tangible media objects like optical disks, USBs, and of course floppy disks are still subject to damage that could make their data unreadable. Optical disks can start to decay after approximately five years, floppy disks are subject to demagnetization, and flash drives can lose their electrical charge.

title: Remembering the Past, Preserving the Present: The America 250 Semiquincentennial Web Archive
content:
The America 250 Semiquincentennial Web Archive documents how Americans are commemorating and reflecting on the nation’s 250th anniversary. In this interview, Malea Walker discusses how the collection evolved from a project focused on government websites into a broader effort to document the many ways communities across the country are marking this historic milestone.  

Please introduce yourself. What is your job at the Library of Congress, and what was your role in creating this collection? 

My name is Malea Walker, and I am a Reference Librarian in the Newspaper and Current Periodical Reading Room. I specialize in government documents, so I initially wanted to start a collection that would archive the websites of all of the America 250 state commissions and the federal government websites that were being created to celebrate the 250th anniversary of the country. With those sites in mind, I proposed the collection in 2023, but when the scope expanded to include other subjects, I became the Collection Leader for a collaborative web archive collection team that includes subject experts from around the Library. 

Can you briefly describe the collection?

title: Vintage Records Meet Novel Technology: Using Artificial Intelligence to Find New Stories for America’s 250th Birthday
content:
This year libraries and cultural institutions around the nation are celebrating America’s 250th birthday. The 225-year-old Library of Congress is almost as old as the country itself and this year we’ve joined forces with the Smithsonian Institution to find new stories about America’s founding in our treasure trove of records and artifacts. 

The collaboration, called Revolution Crossroads, is exploring how advanced technologies can surface new connections in history. Staff are working to expand the promise of artificial intelligence (AI) to surface relationships, stories, and context—using some of the nation’s founding digital treasures as a testbed.

Revolution Crossroads builds on vast collections of Revolutionary Era materials held by the Library, the Smithsonian, and other publicly available materials like those at the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA). These holdings include newspaper articles, letters, military records, 3D objects, maps, artworks, and much more, making the possibilities for investigation using the power of AI especially enticing.

title: “For the Benefit of Humankind:” The Library of Congress and AI for Libraries, Archives and Museums
content:
The Library of Congress recently signed on as a founding member of an international organization devoted to exploring the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in cultural heritage and research contexts “for the benefit of humankind.”  

The Library has been working with the AI4LAM (AI for Libraries, Archives and Museums) organization since soon after its formation in 2018. AI4LAM now has over 40 institutional members from more than 10 countries, representing libraries, research institutions, and museums across the globe.

Library of Congress Chief Information Officer Judith Conklin signed an agreement formally constituting AI4LAM last winter, and now the Library is looking forward to its first co-hosted Fantastic Futures conference this September.  

The growth of this organization from a small network eight years ago to its robust current form indicates the importance of LAM (library, archive, and museum) voices in AI discussions and implementation. As experts in data and technology transformation, practitioners in these organizations hope to ensure that AI adoption is purposeful and responsible.
